Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative unfolds primarily as a continuous, real-time scene—covering the boarding of the three passengers and the brief ferry crossing—complete with vivid sensory details (the vibrating deck, the fog, the squeaking rollers) and concise dialogue that reveals Ilse's stoic character. However, the author skillfully weaves brief moments of exposition and summary into this real-time action. Instead of halting the story for long, dry info-dumps, background details—such as Ilse's forty-one years on the job, the history of giving Kolb's dog a piece of sausage, the cable holding since 1978, and the routine Wednesday phone calls—are seamlessly integrated into the scene as the characters interact with their environment. This balance keeps the pacing steady and engaging while giving the reader a deep sense of history and quiet tension.
